deep.reconstruction:
Hilbert's notebook 600_3, folio 57, contains four separate notes.

(0) Lines 1–2 finish the thought from the previous page. That page studied boundary-value problems y'' = λA(x)y, or nonlinear analogues such as y'' = λA(x)y^2 + B(x)y. It asked whether the 'singular values' (branch points) λ_1, λ_2, … determine A(x), and whether they can be varied freely. Here Hilbert adds that for the nonlinear equation the density of the branch points λ_i is evidently 'different', i.e. it has a different asymptotic distribution than in the linear Sturm–Liouville case. This is a remark, not a derivation.

(1) Calculus of variations. Proposed 'Grundprinzip': an extremal γ of J[y] = ∫F(x,y,y')dx stops being a minimizing function only when two solutions coincide. 'Two solutions' means two extremals through the initial point with the prescribed endpoint. 'Coincide' means at a 'discriminating point', i.e. a zero of the discriminant (the envelope or caustic of the pencil of extremals). In modern terms: minimality persists up to the first point conjugate to the initial point (Jacobi's condition).

Hilbert then asks to bring three facts into the closest connection:
- (i) the second variation can vanish, δ²J[η] = ∫(F_{y'y'}η'^2 + 2F_{yy'}ηη' + F_{yy}η^2)dx = 0 for some η ≠ 0 with η(a) = η(b) = 0;
- (ii) the 'polarized' (linearized) Euler–Lagrange equation has a nontrivial solution vanishing at both ends. This is the Jacobi accessory equation, d/dx(F_{y'y'}η' + F_{yy'}η) − (F_{yy'}η' + F_{yy}η) = 0, i.e. the Euler equation of δ²J. (Taking the variation of the Euler–Lagrange operator in direction η is its polarization.)
- (iii) the family of extremals through the initial point stops being 'developable', i.e. one can no longer construct a Weierstrass field of extremals around γ.

The implicit link (mine): η = ∂y(x,α)/∂α along the pencil of extremals solves (ii). It vanishes at x = a and at the envelope (discriminant) point. Integration by parts gives δ²J[η] = 0. Before that point the pencil simply covers a neighbourhood and defines a field. So (i), (ii), (iii) and 'two solutions coincide' are all the same conjugate-point condition.

(2) First-order PDE F(x,u,∇u) = 0. Hilbert proposes a characterization: characteristics are the curves along which every solution stays regular, i.e. unbranched. Example: the geodesic distance from a point P (a solution of the eikonal equation |∇u| = 1, whose characteristics are geodesics) varies regularly along each geodesic through P. Branching (multivaluedness) occurs only when one leaves the geodesic.

(3) Limit cycles. Take dy/dx = f(x,y) with a Poincaré cycle x = φ(t), y = ψ(t), with φ and ψ 2π-periodic. Task: state the condition for the cycle to be multiple, precisely n-fold. Method: substitute φ + δ(t), ψ + ε(t) and expand in the perturbation, i.e. study the variational equation along the cycle.

Modern reading: the Poincaré return map P on a transversal satisfies P(s) − s = c_n s^n + …. The cycle is n-fold iff P'(0) = 1, P''(0) = … = P^{(n−1)}(0) = 0 and P^{(n)}(0) ≠ 0. The first condition is ∮ div(X,Y) dt = 0 along the cycle. Higher conditions come from the higher-order variational equations.

Hilbert then wants to use this to prove 'my claim of the finite number of cycles'. Presumably the idea is that cycles cannot accumulate because an accumulation cycle would have infinite multiplicity. This is the finiteness half of what became Hilbert's 16th problem, second part.
errors: Written literally as dy/dx = f(x,y) with single-valued f, a closed orbit is impossible unless f has poles at the vertical tangencies. The intended setting is the system x' = X, y' = Y (dy/dx = Y/X), as in Hilbert's 16th problem.

The finiteness claim is false without restrictions. For non-polynomial analytic or smooth f there can be infinitely many limit cycles, and a center (e.g. dy/dx = -x/y) has a continuum of non-isolated cycles of 'infinite multiplicity'. One must restrict to polynomial vector fields and isolated cycles.

The suggested route does not by itself give finiteness. Finite multiplicity of each cycle excludes non-isolatedness but not accumulation of cycles on a polycycle (separatrix cycle). That is exactly the gap in Dulac's 1923 'proof', closed only by Ilyashenko and Écalle (1991–92).

'Minimality persists until two solutions coincide' is heuristically correct (Jacobi). For a strong minimum, however, it also needs the Legendre and Weierstrass conditions; it is not a full sufficiency statement.

The PDE characterization is inverted relative to the standard view. Singularities and discontinuities of solutions propagate along characteristics, so characteristics are where solutions can be non-regular across, not where all solutions stay regular. The geodesic-distance example is also delicate: d(·,P) itself has a cone singularity at P (d² is regular), and branching arises at the cut locus/caustics. The remark is a heuristic, not a correct theorem.

deep.surprise_reason: The variational-calculus and PDE remarks are routine heuristics. The limit-cycle note is a notable unpublished detail. It shows Hilbert explicitly believed he could prove finiteness of limit cycles, and outlined a plan via the multiplicity of cycles obtained by perturbing the periodic solution. This anticipates the Dulac-style approach to the 16th problem. However, the question itself is publicly his (1900 problems), and the plan is only sketched and, as stated, insufficient.

checkable.sympy: x,c,lam,b=symbols('x c lam b'); y=b*exp(c*x**2/2+lam*x); simplify(diff(y,x)-(c*x+lam)*y)==0
checkable.asserts: Example from the previous page: y = b e^{cx²/2+λx} solves y' = (cx+λ)y.
For r' = r(1−r²)², the cycle r = 1 is a double (2-fold) limit cycle: g(1) = 0, g'(1) = 0, g''(1) = 8 ≠ 0.

For x' = −y + x(1−r²), y' = x + y(1−r²), the divergence on r = 1 is 2 − 4r² = −2. Its integral over the period is −4π ≠ 0, so the cycle is simple (hyperbolic). The expression here is an illustrative placeholder: the actual divergence integral to check is integrate(2-4*1, (t,0,2*pi)) = -4*pi.
The center x' = −y, y' = x has every circle as a cycle (non-isolated), a counterexample to unrestricted finiteness.

checkable.sympy: a,s=symbols('a s'); # pencil of geodesics on unit sphere from north pole meet again at antipode s=pi: J''+J=0, J(0)=0 -> J=sin(s); solve(sin(s),s)
checkable.asserts: Jacobi field along a great circle vanishes again at s = π: the conjugate point where 'two solutions coincide', illustrating the variational principle.

Line 9: 'zusammenfallen also bis zu einer discriminirenden Stelle' is correct ('discriminirenden' as in discriminant point).
